limit_of_record: CONTROL: No sovereign sets a tin maximum for drinking water, bottled water or natural mineral water. The drinking-water instrument family carries no tin parameter at all (EU Directive 2020/2184 Annex I Parts B and C; US EPA National Primary Drinking Water Regulations; US FDA 21 CFR 165.110 standards of quality; Health Canada; NHMRC; WHO), and none of the national food-schedule packaged-water lines (Hong Kong Cap 132V, Israel FCS 2016, India FSSAI 2016, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011, GSO 193/2021, Colombia Res 4506/2013, Chile Decreto 977/1996, Fiji FSR 2009) carries a tin entry for water. A read-across is not supportable: the nearest sovereign tin maxima are the canned-food and canned-beverage maximum levels, which exist to bound dissolution of tin from a tinplate container wall into an acidic canned matrix, and the canned-beverage value (100 mg/kg inorganic tin) sits roughly four orders of magnitude above anything a packaged water can plausibly contain, so importing it would publish a ceiling that functions as no limit at all. The dominant packaging for this category (PET, HDPE, glass, aluminium) contains no tin. Natural mineral water is bottled at source in glass or PET; tinplate presentation does not occur in this form. Tin therefore remains a mandatory control cell; no number is invented.

limit_of_record: CONTROL: No credible sovereign government sets a methylmercury maximum level for this product form: authors2025-the-icp-ms-study-on-the-release-of and hwang2022-home-meal-replacement-heavy-metals measured methylmercury in this matrix, so the species is not absent and no not-material determination is supportable. Methylmercury is therefore held under mandatory analytical control rather than recorded not-material, and it remains bounded by identity below the published total-mercury ceiling of 10 ug/kg for this row (methylmercury cannot exceed total mercury). No methylmercury ceiling is invented. INSTRUMENTS CHECKED, so the negative claim is auditable: EU 2023/915 (no methylmercury entry); Codex CXS 193 (none); FSANZ Schedule 19 (none); Health Canada and UK dietary instruments (none); US FDA CPG 540.600, which sets a methylmercury action level of 1000 ug/kg for fish, shellfish, crustaceans and other aquatic animals but not for a composite meal; and HK Cap. 132V, whose methylmercury rows are fish-species rows (fish, fish balls and fish cakes 500; orange roughy 800; pink cusk-eel 1000; tuna 1200; alfonsino 1500; shark 1600; marlin 1700 ug/kg). Every existing value is an aquatic-animal instrument and every one is looser than the 10 ug/kg total-mercury ceiling published on this row, so none could bind even if it were applicable. EVIDENCE TEST, AND WHY THE TWO COMPOSITE ROWS OF THIS CATEGORY RESOLVE METHYLMERCURY DIFFERENTLY. hwang2022-home-meal-replacement-heavy-metals measured methylmercury directly in 480 Korean home-meal-replacement products and reported it BY MATRIX PHASE: detected in the non-fatty solid phase (mean 3.0, maximum 48.0 ug/kg) and the fatty solid phase, and NOT DETECTED in both the non-fatty liquid phase and the fatty liquid phase. A soup, broth or stock is the liquid phase, and a plated frozen dinner is the solid phase. That is why mixed-meals-prepared-foods holds methylmercury under mandatory analytical control (the species was measured in its matrix, so a not-material determination is not supportable there) while this row records a substantiated not-material determination with a reflex trigger. The asymmetry is evidence-driven and is recorded here rather than left to look like an inconsistency. Occurrence evidence is used only to test materiality, never to select a number (Method v2.0).

limit_of_record: CONTROL: Inorganic tin is a tinplate/canned-food migration pathway, not a background dietary contaminant of a frozen or boxed meal. A CANNED prepared meal (canned ravioli, canned chili) is governed by the canned-foods tin ML (Codex CXS 193, 250 mg/kg = 250000 ug/kg); a frozen, chilled, or dry-packaged prepared meal has no tin source. Total tin is reported; a signal on a non-canned form triggers packaging-source investigation. THE STRICTEST APPLICABLE CANNED-FOOD TIN ML IS THE EU ROW AT 200 mg/kg, NOT THE 250 mg/kg FIGURE v1.1 NAMED. Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 sets tin at 200000 ug/kg (200 mg/kg) for canned foods other than canned beverages, except canned dried and canned powdered products (eu2023_sn_canned_foods_200000, basis product as placed on the market). It is stricter than the three rows v1.1 named as converging at 250 mg/kg (codex_cxs193_sn_canned_250000, aunz_sch19_sn_canned_250000, hk_cap132v_sn_canned-food-other-than-canned-beverages_250000), it is a credible-regulator maximum level in a basis this row accepts, and it was neither named nor dispositioned. This defect was found by hand during the v1.2 remediation and NOT by the compiler safety-net, because the soups row's audit_exclude_scope contained the term `beverage`, which matched the phrase 'canned beverages' inside the EU row's own scope string and suppressed it from every scan; the same class of regex self-defeat the v1.2 audit identified elsewhere. The term is removed. The canned form is verified against the EU value, and the EU instrument's own carve-out for canned dried and canned powdered products is independent confirmation that a tin maximum level does not reach a dry soup mix or a bouillon powder. Stricter still, and disclosed rather than adopted because they reach a different form: canned beverages at 100 mg/kg (eu2023_sn_canned_beverages_100000) and at 150 mg/kg (hk_cap132v_sn_canned-beverages_150000). Where a certified product is a canned drinkable broth presented as a beverage rather than a canned food, the canned-beverage value is the applicable one and the stricter of the two applicable rows governs; no single number is asserted across forms.

limit_of_record: CONTROL: No credible regulator sets an aluminium maximum level for a prepared meal or for any principal component of one. Instruments checked: EU 2023/915 and EU 2024/1987 (no aluminium entry), Codex CXS 193 (no aluminium entry), FSANZ Schedule 19 (aluminium appears only as infant-formula MLs of 500 and 1000 ug/kg, which are Category 1 scope), Hong Kong Cap. 132V Part 2 Schedule (no aluminium entry), and US FDA, Health Canada and UK dietary instruments (no aluminium ML). Aluminium reaches the credible register only in three basis families that cannot anchor a food-content cell: drinking-water parametric values (EU 2020/2184 and US 21 CFR 165.110 at 200 ug/L, Health Canada at 2900 ug/L), food-contact-material specific migration limits (EU 10/2011, a migration figure), and toy migration limits. Permitted-additive maxima for aluminium-containing additives in baked goods and starch noodles exist only in non-credible-tier instruments and are additive-use levels rather than contaminant ceilings. Aluminium is therefore a mandatory reported cell with no invented ceiling.

limit_of_record: CONTROL: No jurisdiction sets a tin content limit for any oral-care or cosmetic product; the sovereign tin maximum levels in the register are canned-food and food-contact values written for tinplate migration into food and are a different basis entirely. Tin is additionally not a pure impurity in this category: stannous fluoride and stannous chloride are authorised anticaries and antigingivitis actives in dentifrices and mouthrinses, so a finished-product tin ceiling would be exceeded by design in a compliant stannous formulation and would be meaningless as a contaminant control. The cell is held under mandatory analytical control with a declaration reconciliation rather than declared not-material, because tin is unambiguously present at material levels in this category and an absence claim would be contradicted on its face.

limit_of_record: NOT-MATERIAL: Every tin maximum level in the register is scoped to canned product: EU Reg. 2023/915 sets 200000 ug/kg for canned foods and 100000 ug/kg for canned beverages, Codex CXS 193-1995 and AU-NZ Schedule 19 set 250000 ug/kg for canned foods, and Hong Kong Cap. 132V sets 250000 ug/kg for canned food other than canned beverages. Those limits regulate one contamination pathway, dissolution of tin from tinplate into the packed food. This row is not packed in tinplate, so the pathway that every sovereign tin limit addresses is physically absent and any tin present is dietary background rather than packaging migration. Fresh and frozen vegetables in this row are sold loose, bagged, netted or in polymer trays. Hermetically sealed tinplate presentations of this commodity route to the canned-foods row in Category 7 and carry the canned-foods tin maximum level there.

limit_of_record: CONTROL: No credible sovereign government sets an aluminium contaminant maximum level for any fruit, vegetable or produce form in any jurisdiction. The register's aluminium limits are drinking-water and bottled-water parameters, infant-formula maximum levels, a food-contact plastics specific migration limit, toy migration limits, and permitted-additive levels for baked and starch foods; none of them regulates aluminium as a contaminant of produce. Aluminium is also the third most abundant element in the earth's crust and appears in produce largely as soil-derived and root-associated mineral content rather than as process contamination, so no near-neighbour read-across is supportable either. Under the government-limit-only method HMTc publishes no standalone aluminium number for this row.

limit_of_record: NOT-MATERIAL: No credible sovereign government sets a hexavalent-chromium maximum level for any solid food in any jurisdiction. The register's only INGESTED Cr(VI) parameters are drinking-water maxima (Australia NHMRC 2025, 50 ug/L, nhmrc2025_crvi_drinking_water_50; California SWRCB, 10 ug/L, us_ca_swrcb_2024_cr-vi_chromium-hexavalent_mcl_10ugl and ca_swrcb_crvi_drinking_water_10), which are water-basis parameters expressed per litre of a consumed liquid and supply no applicable ceiling for a solid produce row in this row's native basis; every remaining Cr(VI) row in the register is an article or material limit (toys, textiles, leather, fertilisers, electrical equipment). Chromium in produce is dominated by nutritionally essential Cr(III), and Cr(VI) is not stable in the plant matrix: fruit and vegetable tissue is an aqueous, organic-acid and ascorbate-rich reducing medium in which Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III), so a reported Cr(VI) value in this matrix reflects extraction conditions rather than the chromium species the consumer ingests. Hexavalent chromium is therefore bounded by the published total-chromium screen for this row (Hong Kong Cap. 132V item 7, 500 ug/kg) and controlled by reflex speciation rather than by a published number.

limit_of_record: CONTROL: No sovereign sets a total chromium content limit for a mouth-contact oral-care article. Canada's Consumer Products Containing Lead Regulations (SOR/2018-83), the only instrument scoped to mouth-contact consumer products on a total-content basis, is lead-only — as is the second article-content lead instrument named in this row's own lead cell, REACH Annex XVII entry 63(7) as added by Regulation (EU) 2015/628; the EU toy values (Directive 2009/48 / EN 71-3) are MIGRATION limits and are excluded by this row's basis guard, and finished-cosmetic impurity schedules are written for a formulated product and do not reach an article. The cell is held under mandatory analytical control, not declared not-material: chromium is a defining alloying element of the stainless steel used for staples, wires and tips and is present in chrome plating and in Cr(III) pigments; total chromium is a screen for the Cr(VI) reflex below and is not itself protective.

limit_of_record: NOT-MATERIAL: No credible sovereign government sets a hexavalent-chromium maximum level for any solid food in any jurisdiction. The register's only INGESTED Cr(VI) parameters are drinking-water maxima (Australia NHMRC 2025, 50 ug/L, nhmrc2025_crvi_drinking_water_50; California SWRCB, 10 ug/L, us_ca_swrcb_2024_cr-vi_chromium-hexavalent_mcl_10ugl and ca_swrcb_crvi_drinking_water_10), which are water-basis parameters expressed per litre of a consumed liquid and supply no applicable ceiling for a solid produce row in this row's native basis; every remaining Cr(VI) row in the register is an article or material limit (toys, textiles, leather, fertilisers, electrical equipment). Chromium in produce is dominated by nutritionally essential Cr(III), and Cr(VI) is not stable in the plant matrix: fruit and vegetable tissue is an aqueous, organic-acid and ascorbate-rich reducing medium in which Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III), so a reported Cr(VI) value in this matrix reflects extraction conditions rather than the chromium species the consumer ingests. Hexavalent chromium is therefore bounded by the published total-chromium screen for this row (read-across from Hong Kong Cap. 132V item 7, 500 ug/kg) and controlled by reflex speciation rather than by a published number.

limit_of_record: CONTROL: No credible sovereign government sets an inorganic-arsenic maximum level for terrestrial red-meat muscle tissue. Every credible inorganic-arsenic instrument on the register is scoped elsewhere: EU 2023/915 and EU 2025/1891 to rice, rice products, fruit juices, infant food and seafood; UK, Health Canada and US FDA to rice-based and juice matrices; Hong Kong Cap. 132V to rice and aquatic animals. A NOT-MATERIAL determination is deliberately REJECTED for this cell rather than adopted for convenience: organoarsenical feed additives (roxarsone, nitarsone, arsanilic acid, carbarsone) were lawfully administered to poultry and swine in major producing markets within living memory and are documented to leave arsenic residues in edible tissue, so the programme will not make the affirmative claim that no inorganic-arsenic pathway exists in terrestrial animal food. For the ruminant rows, where no equivalent additive history applies, the absence of that pathway does not by itself substantiate a not-material determination either, because neither a sovereign number nor a supportable near-neighbour analogue exists for the cell in any case. Because no sovereign number governs the cell and no near-neighbour cell is a supportable analogue (a rice or seafood inorganic-arsenic maximum level describes a different contamination mechanism entirely), the cell is a control: testing is mandatory and no ceiling is invented.

limit_of_record: CONTROL: No credible sovereign government sets a hexavalent-chromium content limit for any food, and no near-neighbour read-across is supportable: every credible Cr(VI) instrument on the register is an article, textile, leather, toy-migration, tattoo-ink, fertiliser or electrical-equipment limit written in a non-food basis, and applying one to a poultry-meat matrix would be the basis conflation this row's basis guard exists to reject. No ceiling is invented. THIS CELL WAS PREVIOUSLY CARRIED AS A NOT-MATERIAL DETERMINATION AND THAT DETERMINATION IS WITHDRAWN FOR POULTRY, for two independent reasons. First, the reference-method evidence behind the reduction argument does not reach this matrix. That argument (Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) by tissue reductants and does not persist, so a reported Cr(VI) figure is an artifact of the extraction chemistry) rests on saraiva2021, species-specific isotope-dilution HPLC-ICP-MS, in which Cr(VI) was unquantified in every sample and spiked Cr(VI) was reduced essentially completely during workup. That study covers bovine meat, infant formula milk and semi-skimmed milk. It does not cover poultry. A not-material claim is an affirmative claim and may not be extended by analogy to a matrix the underlying method study never examined; it continues to support the beef, pork and lamb rows, where the matrix was directly measured. Second, the routed corpus contradicts the claim for this exact row. mahmud2011-crvi-chicken-pakistan (peer-reviewed, B-tier) reports author-declared Cr(VI) means of 0.233 to 1.266 mg/kg across chicken meat parts (leg muscle highest at 1.266 mg/kg) and 0.323 to 1.433 mg/kg across bones (head bone highest). The muscle-meat figures alone reach 1.27 times this row's own total-chromium screen of 1 mg/kg, and the row is scoped to muscle meat, so the exceedance does not depend on the bone values.  The paper and attributes them to a documented mechanical supply-chain pathway: chrome-tanned leather offcuts fed to poultry as cheap protein, carrying residual hexavalent chromium from K2CrO4 and K2Cr2O7 tanning liquors. The routed occurrence pool for poultry-product|Cr-VI is not quarantined and carries a stable sensitivity band. The programme records openly that mahmud2011 is weak evidence of SPECIATION: muffle-furnace ashing and nitric-acid digestion followed by atomic absorption calibrated against potassium dichromate, with no chromatographic separation and no speciation-preservation validation, measures total chromium irrespective of oxidation state, and the reported values sit in the same range as the total-chromium screen, which is what a total-chromium measurement mislabelled as Cr(VI) would look like. That caveat is why this cell does not publish a number derived from those values, and it could not in any case: occurrence never selects an HMTc limit. But the FEED-INPUT PATHWAY the paper documents is not an analytical artifact, and the correct response to a real pathway measured by an inadequate method is to require an adequate method, not to declare the analyte not material. Under the programme's fail-safe rule a cell in this position is a control.

limit_of_record: CONTROL: No credible sovereign government sets an inorganic-arsenic maximum level for formulated processed meat. Every credible inorganic-arsenic instrument on the register is scoped elsewhere: EU 2023/915 and EU 2025/1891 to rice, rice products, fruit juices, infant food and seafood; UK, Health Canada and US FDA to rice-based and juice matrices; Hong Kong Cap. 132V to rice and aquatic animals. A NOT-MATERIAL determination is deliberately REJECTED for this cell rather than adopted for convenience: organoarsenical feed additives (roxarsone, nitarsone, arsanilic acid, carbarsone) were lawfully administered to poultry and swine in major producing markets within living memory and are documented to leave arsenic residues in edible tissue, so the programme will not make the affirmative claim that no inorganic-arsenic pathway exists in terrestrial animal food. For the ruminant rows, where no equivalent additive history applies, the absence of that pathway does not by itself substantiate a not-material determination either, because neither a sovereign number nor a supportable near-neighbour analogue exists for the cell in any case. Because no sovereign number governs the cell and no near-neighbour cell is a supportable analogue (a rice or seafood inorganic-arsenic maximum level describes a different contamination mechanism entirely), the cell is a control: testing is mandatory and no ceiling is invented.

limit_of_record: NOT-MATERIAL: Hexavalent chromium is not stable in this matrix. A formulated processed-meat product is a wet, reducing, protein- and thiol-rich medium; Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) by tissue reductants (cysteine, glutathione, ascorbate) and by the acid and heat of digestion and cooking, so a Cr(VI) figure reported on such a matrix is an artifact of the extraction chemistry of the total-chromium screen rather than a measurement of a species that persists in the food. The determination follows the same reference-method adjudication recorded for the hexavalent-chromium cell in the infant-formula category (data/workbench standards Cr-VI adjudication), applied here to an animal-tissue matrix. Hexavalent chromium is in any event a species of, and bounded by, the published total-chromium screen (Cr-VI <= total Cr). SCOPE OF THIS DETERMINATION — POULTRY CARVE-OUT: this not-material determination rests on the red-meat matrix evidence (saraiva2021, bovine meat) and is NOT extended to a poultry-containing formulation. Where the declared formulation contains poultry, the lot inherits the poultry-product row's hexavalent-chromium control in full, including the mandatory EN 15192 / EPA 6800 determination and the supplier feed-input declaration covering chrome-tanned leather and tannery-waste protein. See the poultry-product Cr-VI cell for the withdrawal record and the mahmud2011-crvi-chicken-pakistan pathway evidence behind it.

Those limits regulate one contamination pathway, dissolution of tin from tinplate into the packed food. This row is not packed in tinplate, so the pathway that every sovereign tin limit addresses is physically absent and any tin present is dietary background rather than packaging migration. Fresh and frozen roots and tubers are sold loose, netted, bagged or in polymer trays. Hermetically sealed tinplate presentations of this commodity route to the canned-foods row in Category 7 and carry the canned-foods tin maximum level there.

limit_of_record: CONTROL: No credible sovereign government sets an aluminium contaminant maximum level for any fruit, vegetable or produce form in any jurisdiction. The register's aluminium limits are drinking-water and bottled-water parameters, infant-formula maximum levels, a food-contact plastics specific migration limit, toy migration limits, and permitted-additive levels for baked and starch foods; none of them regulates aluminium as a contaminant of produce. Aluminium is also the third most abundant element in the earth's crust and appears in produce largely as soil-derived and root-associated mineral content rather than as process contamination, so no near-neighbour read-across is supportable either. Under the government-limit-only method HMTc publishes no standalone aluminium number for this row.

limit_of_record: NOT-MATERIAL: No credible sovereign government sets a hexavalent-chromium maximum level for any solid food in any jurisdiction. The register's only INGESTED Cr(VI) parameters are drinking-water maxima (Australia NHMRC 2025, 50 ug/L, nhmrc2025_crvi_drinking_water_50; California SWRCB, 10 ug/L, us_ca_swrcb_2024_cr-vi_chromium-hexavalent_mcl_10ugl and ca_swrcb_crvi_drinking_water_10), which are water-basis parameters expressed per litre of a consumed liquid and supply no applicable ceiling for a solid produce row in this row's native basis; every remaining Cr(VI) row in the register is an article or material limit (toys, textiles, leather, fertilisers, electrical equipment). Chromium in produce is dominated by nutritionally essential Cr(III), and Cr(VI) is not stable in the plant matrix: fruit and vegetable tissue is an aqueous, organic-acid and ascorbate-rich reducing medium in which Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III), so a reported Cr(VI) value in this matrix reflects extraction conditions rather than the chromium species the consumer ingests. Hexavalent chromium is therefore bounded by the published total-chromium screen for this row (Hong Kong Cap. 132V item 7, 500 ug/kg) and controlled by reflex speciation rather than by a published number.

limit_of_record: CONTROL: No credible sovereign sets a total-arsenic maximum level for a soft drink or carbonated beverage. Regulators write beverage arsenic limits on the inorganic species (EU 2023/915 section 3.4.4 fruit juices at 20 ug/kg and section 3.4.1.6 non-alcoholic rice-based drinks at 30 ug/kg; the US FDA apple-juice action level at 10 ug/kg) and write unspeciated arsenic limits only in the packaged-water and public-water-supply schedules, which are Category 8 instruments. The inorganic-arsenic cell in this row carries the health-relevant fraction. Total arsenic is therefore mandatory on every lot as the parent screen and no total-arsenic ceiling is invented.

The only sovereign aluminium values in a dietary basis are the packaged-drinking-water quality standards (US 21 CFR 165.110 secondary allowable level 200 ug/kg, EU 2020/2184, Health Canada 2900 ug/kg), which govern water sold as water and are Category 8 instruments, and the FSANZ infant-formula aluminium limits, which are Category 1 and are excluded from this category's anchor set by the taxonomy boundary rule. In this form aluminium is a packaging and processing signal (aluminium cans and can linings, closures, filter aids, additive carry-over) rather than a raw-material contaminant. Aluminium is a live cell for this row because the dominant packaging format is the aluminium can and because a low-pH carbonated formulation is exactly the condition under which a compromised can lining leaches, so the tripwire is a packaging-integrity control as well as an ingredient control.

limit_of_record: NOT-MATERIAL: Hexavalent chromium is not stable in a carbonated or still soft drink. At the pH of this product form (typically pH 2.4 to 3.5, with phosphoric, citric and carbonic acid and invert or high-fructose sugars present in the formulation) Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) by the organic acids, sugars, ascorbate and polyphenols present in the matrix, so a positive Cr(VI) result is an artifact of the total-chromium determination rather than a species present in the beverage as consumed. The reference-method basis for this determination is the in-house species arbitration at data/workbench/standards/2026-07-31-chromium-formula-adjudication.md, which found that the superseded ion-exchange plus electrothermal-AAS methods that generated the historical Cr(VI) values in liquid food matrices are not reproduced by the modern reference method: saraiva2021 (species-specific isotope dilution HPLC-ICP-MS, limit of quantification 0.049 ug/kg) quantified no Cr(VI) in any milk or formula sample while resolving Cr(III) and total chromium at single-digit ug/kg. That adjudication was drawn on a near-neutral aqueous food matrix; the acidic beverage matrices in this row are a more strongly reducing environment still, so the artifact conclusion carries a fortiori. The health-relevant species is controlled through the total-chromium cell and the reflex rule below, and this determination is a method finding, not an occurrence-derived value: no number is taken from it.

limit_of_record: CONTROL: Inorganic tin is a tinplate migration pathway confined to the canned form, and three of the four forms this row certifies are not canned foods. The subcategory as scoped covers canned soups, dry soup mixes, bouillon cubes and powders, and ready-to-drink carton stocks and broths; the canned-foods tin maximum level reaches only the first. v1.1 published that ML as a row-wide firm ceiling of 250 mg/kg while its own label conceded that dry-mix, bouillon and carton-RTD forms have no tin migration pathway, so the compiled record asserted a 250 mg/kg tin ceiling for a carton broth that no instrument sets and the publication gate counted it as a firm protective limit. v1.2 converts the cell to the control + companion_ml pattern the other two rows of this category already use (mixed-meals-prepared-foods and bone-broth), so the canned form is verified against the ML while no ceiling is asserted for the forms the instrument does not reach. A form-split cell was considered and is not available in this compiler. A CANNED soup is verified against the canned-foods tin ML, on which three credible regulators converge at 250 mg/kg (250000 ug/kg): Codex CXS 193 (canned foods), FSANZ Schedule 19 (all canned foods) and HK Cap. 132V (canned food other than canned beverages), so the figure is not a single-jurisdiction artefact. The Cap. 132V canned-beverage row (150 mg/kg) is stricter but is not adopted: a ready-to-drink carton stock is not a canned beverage and has no tinplate contact, and a canned soup is a canned food under every one of these instruments. Instruments checked for the non-canned forms: EU 2023/915 (tin appears only as canned-food and canned-beverage MLs), Codex CXS 193, FSANZ Schedule 19, Cap. 132V, US FDA, Health Canada and UK dietary instruments; none sets a tin maximum level for a dry soup mix, a bouillon cube or a carton broth. THE STRICTEST APPLICABLE CANNED-FOOD TIN ML IS THE EU ROW AT 200 mg/kg, NOT THE 250 mg/kg FIGURE v1.1 NAMED. Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 sets tin at 200000 ug/kg (200 mg/kg) for canned foods other than canned beverages, except canned dried and canned powdered products (eu2023_sn_canned_foods_200000, basis product as placed on the market). It is stricter than the three rows v1.1 named as converging at 250 mg/kg (codex_cxs193_sn_canned_250000, aunz_sch19_sn_canned_250000, hk_cap132v_sn_canned-food-other-than-canned-beverages_250000), it is a credible-regulator maximum level in a basis this row accepts, and it was neither named nor dispositioned. This defect was found by hand during the v1.2 remediation and NOT by the compiler safety-net, because the soups row's audit_exclude_scope contained the term `beverage`, which matched the phrase 'canned beverages' inside the EU row's own scope string and suppressed it from every scan; the same class of regex self-defeat the v1.2 audit identified elsewhere. The term is removed. The canned form is verified against the EU value, and the EU instrument's own carve-out for canned dried and canned powdered products is independent confirmation that a tin maximum level does not reach a dry soup mix or a bouillon powder. Stricter still, and disclosed rather than adopted because they reach a different form: canned beverages at 100 mg/kg (eu2023_sn_canned_beverages_100000) and at 150 mg/kg (hk_cap132v_sn_canned-beverages_150000). Where a certified product is a canned drinkable broth presented as a beverage rather than a canned food, the canned-beverage value is the applicable one and the stricter of the two applicable rows governs; no single number is asserted across forms.

limit_of_record: NOT-MATERIAL: No credible sovereign government sets a hexavalent-chromium maximum level for any solid food in any jurisdiction. The register's only INGESTED Cr(VI) parameters are drinking-water maxima (Australia NHMRC 2025, 50 ug/L, nhmrc2025_crvi_drinking_water_50; California SWRCB, 10 ug/L, us_ca_swrcb_2024_cr-vi_chromium-hexavalent_mcl_10ugl and ca_swrcb_crvi_drinking_water_10), which are water-basis parameters expressed per litre of a consumed liquid and supply no applicable ceiling for a solid produce row in this row's native basis; every remaining Cr(VI) row in the register is an article or material limit (toys, textiles, leather, fertilisers, electrical equipment). Chromium in produce is dominated by nutritionally essential Cr(III), and Cr(VI) is not stable in the plant matrix: fruit and vegetable tissue is an aqueous, organic-acid and ascorbate-rich reducing medium in which Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III), so a reported Cr(VI) value in this matrix reflects extraction conditions rather than the chromium species the consumer ingests. Hexavalent chromium is therefore bounded by the published total-chromium screen for this row (Hong Kong Cap. 132V item 7, 500 ug/kg) and controlled by reflex speciation rather than by a published number.

limit_of_record: NOT-MATERIAL: Hexavalent chromium is not stable in a formulated sports or energy beverage. At the pH of this product form (typically pH 2.5 to 3.8, with citric, phosphoric, malic and ascorbic acid present in the formulation) Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) by the organic acids, sugars, ascorbate and polyphenols present in the matrix, so a positive Cr(VI) result is an artifact of the total-chromium determination rather than a species present in the beverage as consumed. The reference-method basis for this determination is the in-house species arbitration at data/workbench/standards/2026-07-31-chromium-formula-adjudication.md, which found that the superseded ion-exchange plus electrothermal-AAS methods that generated the historical Cr(VI) values in liquid food matrices are not reproduced by the modern reference method: saraiva2021 (species-specific isotope dilution HPLC-ICP-MS, limit of quantification 0.049 ug/kg) quantified no Cr(VI) in any milk or formula sample while resolving Cr(III) and total chromium at single-digit ug/kg. That adjudication was drawn on a near-neutral aqueous food matrix; the acidic beverage matrices in this row are a more strongly reducing environment still, so the artifact conclusion carries a fortiori. The health-relevant species is controlled through the total-chromium cell and the reflex rule below, and this determination is a method finding, not an occurrence-derived value: no number is taken from it.

limit_of_record: CONTROL: No sovereign sets a total chromium content limit for a mouth-contact oral-care article. Canada's Consumer Products Containing Lead Regulations (SOR/2018-83), the only instrument scoped to mouth-contact consumer products on a total-content basis, is lead-only — as is the second article-content lead instrument named in this row's own lead cell, REACH Annex XVII entry 63(7) as added by Regulation (EU) 2015/628; the EU toy values (Directive 2009/48 / EN 71-3) are MIGRATION limits and are excluded by this row's basis guard, and finished-cosmetic impurity schedules are written for a formulated product and do not reach an article. The cell is held under mandatory analytical control, not declared not-material: chromium is a defining alloying element of the stainless steel used for staples, wires and tips and is present in chrome plating and in Cr(III) pigments; total chromium is a screen for the Cr(VI) reflex below and is not itself protective.

basis: acid-soluble / MIGRATED element from accessible toy material (EN 71-3 / ISO 8124-3 0.07 M HCl, 37 C, mg/kg of material). The three instruments in this family state the same measured quantity in three phrasings: Directive 2009/48/EC point 13 element migration, which IS split by material category and whose applicable member here is the Category III (scraped-off material) value; ASTM F963-17 4.3.5 soluble (migrated) element; and NOM-252-SSA1-2011 bioavailable soluble element. The ASTM and NOM-252 limits are not EN 71-3 material-category scoped, so where one of them binds, the published ceiling carries no material-category qualifier. A migration ceiling, not a total-content ceiling.

limit_of_record: NOT-MATERIAL: No sovereign toy-safety instrument sets an inorganic-arsenic limit. Directive 2009/48/EC Annex II Part III point 13, EN 71-3, ISO 8124-3:2020 Table 1, ASTM F963-17 4.3.5 and NOM-252-SSA1-2011 Table 1 all regulate TOTAL arsenic migration from toy material; inorganic arsenic is a dietary speciation with no article-migration counterpart. Arsenic in a wood, wood-composite, plastic or metal chest surface and its finish is bounded by the published total-arsenic migration ceiling by identity (iAs <= tAs), so a separate inorganic-arsenic ceiling would add no control.

limit_of_record: CONTROL: No credible sovereign sets a cadmium maximum level for tea leaf. No credible sovereign sets a cadmium maximum level for tea. Hong Kong Cap 132V names the commodity for lead but not for cadmium, and EU 2023/915, Codex CXS 193, FSANZ Schedule 19 and Health Canada set no tea cell at all. The EU leaf-vegetable cadmium cell (100 ug/kg) is a fresh-weight value for a vegetable eaten whole and cannot be carried onto a dried leaf without an invented drying factor. No near-neighbour read-across is supportable, so the fail-safe disposition is a control: cadmium testing is mandatory on every certified lot and no ceiling is invented from occurrence data.

problems: No numeric or bounded limit-of-record; named method LOQ or defensible read-across required

limit_of_record: CONTROL: No credible sovereign sets a total-arsenic maximum level for tea leaf. Regulators write beverage arsenic limits on the inorganic species (EU 2023/915 section 3.4.4 fruit juices at 20 ug/kg and section 3.4.1.6 non-alcoholic rice-based drinks at 30 ug/kg; the US FDA apple-juice action level at 10 ug/kg) and write unspeciated arsenic limits only in the packaged-water and public-water-supply schedules, which are Category 8 instruments. No sovereign writes an inorganic-arsenic cell for tea either, so both arsenic cells in this row are controls and the escalation rule carries the obligation. Total arsenic is therefore mandatory on every lot as the parent screen and no total-arsenic ceiling is invented.

limit_of_record: CONTROL: No credible sovereign sets an inorganic-arsenic maximum level for tea leaf. Every sovereign inorganic-arsenic cell is scoped either to rice and rice-based products, to a ready-to-drink beverage (EU fruit juices 20 ug/kg, EU non-alcoholic rice-based drinks 30 ug/kg, US FDA apple juice 10 ug/kg), to seafood, or to packaged and public drinking water. None of those is applicable to this dry commodity, and applying a ready-to-drink beverage cell to a dry leaf, bean or powder would be a basis conflation. Inorganic arsenic is a Tier-1 analyte, so it is speciated whenever the total-arsenic screen is elevated.

limit_of_record: NOT-MATERIAL: Hexavalent chromium is not stable in a non-root vegetable juice. At the pH of this product form (typically pH 3.9 to 4.6 for tomato-based juices and mildly acidic for other non-root vegetable juices, with organic acids and ascorbate present) Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) by the organic acids, sugars, ascorbate and polyphenols present in the matrix, so a positive Cr(VI) result is an artifact of the total-chromium determination rather than a species present in the beverage as consumed. The reference-method basis for this determination is the in-house species arbitration at data/workbench/standards/2026-07-31-chromium-formula-adjudication.md, which found that the superseded ion-exchange plus electrothermal-AAS methods that generated the historical Cr(VI) values in liquid food matrices are not reproduced by the modern reference method: saraiva2021 (species-specific isotope dilution HPLC-ICP-MS, limit of quantification 0.049 ug/kg) quantified no Cr(VI) in any milk or formula sample while resolving Cr(III) and total chromium at single-digit ug/kg. That adjudication was drawn on a near-neutral aqueous food matrix; the acidic beverage matrices in this row are a more strongly reducing environment still, so the artifact conclusion carries a fortiori. The health-relevant species is controlled through the total-chromium cell and the reflex rule below, and this determination is a method finding, not an occurrence-derived value: no number is taken from it.

limit_of_record: CONTROL: No jurisdiction sets a tin content limit for any oral-care or cosmetic product; the sovereign tin maximum levels in the register are canned-food and food-contact values written for tinplate migration into food and are a different basis entirely. Tin is additionally not a pure impurity in this category: stannous fluoride and stannous chloride are authorised anticaries and antigingivitis actives in dentifrices and mouthrinses, so a finished-product tin ceiling would be exceeded by design in a compliant stannous formulation and would be meaningless as a contaminant control. The cell is held under mandatory analytical control with a declaration reconciliation rather than declared not-material, because tin is unambiguously present at material levels in this category and an absence claim would be contradicted on its face.
